name: Gargi
role: Vedic woman philosopher of the Upanishads
summary: Gargi Vachaknavi is a woman scholar of the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad who questions the sage Yajnavalkya at King Janaka's great assembly, in two rounds of bold questions.
about: In the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, Gargi Vachaknavi is a learned woman, called a brahmavadini, who stands up at a grand sacrifice held by King Janaka of Videha. The text says Yajnavalkya had claimed a prize of cows, and a series of scholars tested him. Gargi asks what each layer of the world is woven upon, climbing from water and air up to the highest realms, until Yajnavalkya tells her to stop pressing about the deity. Later she returns with two sharp questions about what lies beyond everything, and the answer is the Imperishable. She then tells the Brahmins that none of them can defeat him in speaking of Brahman. Tradition counts her among the nine gems of Janaka's court. Scholars date her roughly between 800 and 500 BCE, and some texts that name a Gargi as Yajnavalkya's wife may speak of a different woman.
kidSummary: Gargi lived long ago in Mithila and loved big questions. At a great gathering of scholars, she bravely asked the wise sage Yajnavalkya what the whole world rests upon. Her questions went deeper and deeper, and people still remember her as a brilliant thinker.

story.title: A prize for the wisest
story.text: King Janaka holds a big festival and sets out a thousand cows, each with gold coins on its horns, for the wisest scholar. Yajnavalkya has the cows driven to his home, and the other scholars come forward to test him.

story.title: Gargi rises
story.text: After several scholars have asked their questions, Gargi Vachaknavi stands up. She asks politely and without fear, and the whole hall listens.

story.title: Layer upon layer
story.text: She asks what the world is woven upon. Water, she hears, rests on air, and air on the sky, and she keeps asking about each next layer, all the way up to the highest worlds.

story.title: A gentle warning
story.text: Yajnavalkya tells her not to ask too far about the deity, because some things cannot be reached by reasoning alone. Gargi respects this and falls silent for a while.

story.title: Two more questions
story.text: She returns and asks two last questions, as sharp as two arrows. The answer is the Imperishable, which holds up even space itself. She then tells everyone that no one can beat Yajnavalkya in speaking of Brahman.

teaches: Keep asking brave and thoughtful questions
Learning belongs to anyone who seeks it
Know when to listen and accept an answer

facts.text: King Janaka offered one thousand cows, each with ten gold coins tied to its horns, as a prize for the most learned scholar at his big sacrifice.
Before anyone else had claimed the prize, Yajnavalkya told his pupil to drive the cows home, which upset the other Brahmins and led to the debate.
Her first questions climb like a ladder: what holds water, then air, sky, the Gandharva worlds, sun, moon, stars, gods, Indra, Prajapati, and finally the worlds of Brahma, each resting on the next.
Gargi uses a weaving picture: each layer of the universe is said to be woven across the next, like thread running through cloth.
When Gargi pushes on, Yajnavalkya warns her that her head might fall off, as the deity she asks about is beyond reasoning; Shankara's commentary adds that it is known only through scripture.

For her second round, Gargi asks the Brahmins' permission and compares herself to a warrior of Kashi or Videha with a strung bow and two sharp arrows; she bows to Yajnavalkya and tells him to be ready for her two questions.
He says that under the rule of the Imperishable the sun and moon keep their places, seasons and years run on, and some rivers flow east while others flow west.
Shyam Ranganathan notes that Gargi is the only questioner who challenges Yajnavalkya twice, and tradition counts her among the Navaratnas, the nine gems of Janaka's court.
Before Gargi's turn, the priest Ashvala, Artabhaga, Bhujyu, Ushasta and Uddalaka had each debated Yajnavalkya and lost.
Yajnavalkya describes the Imperishable only by what it is not: not long or short, not red, not a shadow, with no eyes, ears, speech or mind, and neither an inside nor an outside.
In Shankara's reading, Gargi's follow-up about what space rests on squeezes Yajnavalkya: a plain answer would look like ignorance or a contradiction, so he points to the Imperishable instead.
Yajnavalkya tells her that anyone who performs rites and austerities for thousands of years without knowing the Imperishable earns only limited, perishable results.
In Shankara's commentary, the sun and moon keeping their courses are like a kingdom under a good king: the order of the world points to a ruler, just as a lamp points to its maker.
Shankara notes that fire is missing from Gargi's chain of elements because it cannot show itself alone and needs earth or water, a small puzzle hidden inside her questions.
In the same debate, the kind of warning Gargi heard comes true for another challenger: Vidagdha Shakalya cannot answer Yajnavalkya's last question, and the text says his head fell off.
King Janaka's yajna, where Gargi spoke, is described as lasting many days, with sandalwood, ghee and barley fed to the fire and sages, kings and princes invited from all over India.
In Wikipedia's retelling of the Janaka debate, Gargi is the first speaker to bring up the idea of Brahman, which is why her questions are seen as reaching the heart of the contest.
Gargi has appeared on Indian television: Richa Soni played her in Star Plus's Siya Ke Ram (2015-16), and Meenakshi Sethi in Swastik Productions' Shrimad Ramayan.
A statue of Gargi stands in the complex of the Uchchaith Bhagawati Mandir near Benipatti town, in Bihar's Madhubani district, part of the Mithila region.
A much later yoga text shows a Gargi who is Yajnavalkya's wife and asks easy questions, but scholar Shyam Ranganathan thinks she is a different woman from the Upanishad's debater.

quiz.q: Who was Gargi Vachaknavi questioning at King Janaka's assembly?
quiz.why: Her debates in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad are with Yajnavalkya.

quiz.q: What picture does Gargi use for how the world is held together?
quiz.why: She asks what each layer is woven upon.

quiz.q: What did Gargi compare her two last questions to?
quiz.why: She called them like a warrior's two arrows.

quiz.q: What did Gargi say the other scholars should be glad to do?
options: Escape just by bowing to Yajnavalkya
Ask the king for more gold
quiz.why: She told them they should count it a gain to get off by bowing to him.

quiz.q: What was the prize at Janaka's sacrifice?
quiz.why: Janaka offered a thousand cows with gold coins on their horns.
